Computer Science and Game Theory
☆ Cutting a Cake For Human Consumption: An Elementary $n$-agent Cake Cutting Protocol
Alexandros Psomas
We give a bounded envy-free cake-cutting protocol for any number $n$ of agents in the Robertson--Webb model, with a short, self-contained, and elementary correctness proof. The protocol uses $2^{O(n \log n)}$ queries. Most ingredients are already known and well understood in the fair division literature; our main contribution is a simpler organization of these ideas into a protocol whose complete description and proof fit in a few pages.
☆ A Quasipolynomial Algorithm for $\ell_\infty$ Contractions
Ashkan Soleymani, Gabriele Farina
We give an algorithm for computing an $\eps$-approximate fixed point of any $d$-dimensional nonexpansion with respect to the $\ell_\infty$ norm in time $\log(1/\eps)^{O(\log^2 d)}$. At its core, our method uses a boosting argument to geometrically shrink a search region. Among other consequences, our algorithm implies that simple stochastic games can be solved in quasipolynomial time.
☆ Nashtopes and their A-discriminants
Elke Neuhaus, Irem Portakal, Luca Sodomaco, Katherine Tung
An $n$-player game in normal form is said to be of format $\boldsymbol{d} = (d_1, \dots, d_n)$ if the $i$-th player has $d_i$ options for $1 \le i \le n$, and is said to be balanced if $d_n - 1 \le \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(d_i - 1)$. The Nash equilibria of the game correspond to solutions of the system of indifference equations for the game, with payoff differences as coefficients and strategy probabilities as variables. As such, the mixed discriminant of this system gives some information about which games could have an unusual number of totally mixed Nash equilibria. This mixed discriminant can be regarded as an $\mathcal{A}$-discriminant for some matrix $\mathcal{A}$ in the sense of [Gelfand--Kapranov--Zelevinsky 1994], and the convex hull of the columns of $\mathcal{A}$ is a polytope, which we call the Nashtope. We study this $\mathcal{A}$-discriminant for each balanced game format with at least three players. This discriminant is a subset of the Nash discriminant variety introduced in [Abo--Portakal--Sodomaco 2026]. We compute the codimension and degree of this discriminant for all balanced game formats, including on-boundary formats, using the Euler obstruction formula in [Matsui--Takeuchi 2011]. Our $\mathcal{A}$-discriminant locus corresponds to a special multigraded Hurwitz locus studied in [Pratt--Sodomaco--Sturmfels 2026]. As a consequence of [Pokidkin 2026], we obtain the codimensions and degrees of the irreducible components of the Nash discriminant variety for each balanced game format with at least three players, fully resolving Problem 3.8 of [Abo--Portakal--Sodomaco 2026].
comment: 36 pages, 4 tables. Supplementary software documentation is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23190651
☆ Computing the Nucleon of Matching Games
Haris Aziz, Gergely Csáji
The nucleon is the multiplicative counterpart of the nucleolus: it lexicographically maximizes the fraction of its stand-alone value that each coalition receives. We study exact nucleon computation in matching games and in two extensions: $b$-matching games, in which players may have several partners, and partitioned matching games, in which one player may own several vertices. We resolve three open problems from a recent survey. For ordinary matching games with nonnegative rational weights, we give a polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm using maximum-weight matching, shortest paths, and minimum-cost flow, ; it returns both a nucleon allocation and a compact description of the full nucleon. In contrast, computing any nucleon allocation is NP-hard for unit-weight $b$-matching games with capacities at most three and for unit-weight partitioned matching games of width at most three. Finally, for the unresolved capacity-two case, we show that exact nucleon computation is polynomial-time Turing reducible to SHORTEST NON-ZERO CYCLE.
☆ Formalizing Cooperation and Competition: An AI-Assisted Mathematical Addendum to a 2018 Planning Thesis
Haitham Masaud Amar
We present an AI-assisted mathematical addendum to Strategic Trip Planning: Striking a Balance Between Competition and Cooperation (Amar, 2018). We reconstruct selected relationships between strategic choice, cooperative stability, participant approval and enforcement. The thesis's Nash-to-core proposition is under-specified until outsider opportunities are stated. We verify two-person implications under fixed outsiders and explicit efficiency conditions. Under isolation, the original example has an empty TU core; its funded counterpart uses an explicit external subsidy. For a monotone resource model we characterize the exact financing gap. A finite negotiation procedure implemented in Lean is proved to terminate with participant approval, joint-cost non-worsening and local optimality against permitted approved moves. Supporting formalizations address bargaining geometry and regret-based efficiency. A resource-game counterinstance shows why monotonicity alone provides no uniform price-of-anarchy bound. Reproducible computations compare a documented heuristic reconstruction with the verified procedure on 44 source-based instances and 96 starting cases from four additional synthetic network families. Acceptance-matched heuristic and randomized pairwise-search controls contextualize the optimization results. The mathematical ingredients are established results; the contribution is a traceable reconstruction linking source statements, explicit assumptions, checked proofs, executable code and retained counterinstances. The study illustrates how AI-assisted investigation can turn engineering intuitions from legacy research into precise mathematical claims whose conditions and computational consequences can be inspected and reproduced.
comment: 24 pages, 4 figures. Mathematical addendum to the author's 2018 University of Waterloo PhD thesis. Includes Lean 4 formalization and reproducible synthetic experiments as ancillary material
☆ GSP Autobidding Equilibria with Few Advertisers or Slots
Yiyang Huang, Zhengyang Liu, Yonglei Yan, Zihe Wang
In sponsored-shopping auctions, one advertiser may win several positions, and a product that is never displayed may determine the prices of several winners. Under generalized second-price (GSP) pricing without self-pricing, these interactions couple allocation and payment through a single global ranking. We prove that exact autobidding equilibria under budget and return-on-investment (ROI) constraints can be computed in polynomial time whenever either the number $n$ of advertisers or the number $K$ of display slots is fixed. Our algorithms rely on two structural reductions. With few advertisers, the payment polytopes of tied bid layers combine by a Minkowski sum, giving a fixed-dimensional representation of exponentially many rankings. With few slots, budget equilibria admit threshold recovery and an exact submodular description of attainable payments at the display boundary. For ROI, we prove that every group-consecutive equilibrium has a representative with at most $K+2$ nonunit multipliers, preserving the item and price in every displayed slot. In each case, the reduction leads to polynomially many systems of polynomial equations and inequalities in bounded dimension. The algorithms compute exact multipliers and explicit distributions over valid group-consecutive rankings, with support at most $n+1$; for ROI with few slots, this improves to $\min\{n+1,K+3\}$.
comment: 1 figure, 1 table, 4 algorithms
☆ When Are We Near Nash? Certifying Solutions in General-Sum Games
Boning Li, Longbo Huang
Heuristic solvers for general-sum extensive-form games produce a stream of iterates, and practice reports the NashGap of the returned profile. We ask what a solver can know about its own iterates from the regret accumulators and the terminal-distribution accumulators its updates already maintain. In two-player games the NashGap of a weighted average strategy equals, at the maximizing player, the weighted external regret plus a signed value correction. Bounding the regret by the running counterfactual-regret accumulator gives an online certificate whose cost per checkpoint is linear in the number of terminal histories. The certificate stays sound under alternating updates and in games with three or more players. The mismatch between what alternation evaluates and what the averages record enters as one signed comparator term, maximized in a single backward pass per player whose comparator weight is nonzero. The bound is read off the regret state, with no best response against the average. Run a portfolio of training-free regret-matching solvers, output the iterate with the smallest certificate, and verify that iterate once. On the benchmark's biased Leduc family a pool of sixteen training-free solvers, seven original and nine recent variants, solves $89\%$ of the $64$ instances at threshold $10^{-5}$ this way, matching the trajectory-minimum union of the solvers. The same protocol solves $92\%$ of the $64$ pre-registered held-out instances and $89\%$ again on a third set of $64$ instances that no earlier stage used. The zero-best-response certificate certifies all $57$ in-sample solves and all $57$ fresh ones, and $58$ of the $59$ held-out ones. Its exact-comparator refinement certifies every solve in the three sets. The certificate states both and attributes its bound. Code is available at https://github.com/lbn187/CertNE.
comment: 35 pages, 5 figures
☆ Pareto Inefficiency of EFX
Sepideh Mahabadi, Prasanna Ramakrishnan, Jakub Tarnawski
We consider the problem of allocating indivisible goods to agents with additive valuations, under two classic notions of fairness and efficiency: envy-freeness up to any good (EFX) and Pareto optimality. While some of the earliest work on EFX showed that Pareto optimal EFX allocations may not exist if agents can have zero value for some goods, it has remained open whether the same is true when all values are positive. We present a simple instance in which every good has positive value to every agent, but no Pareto optimal EFX allocation exists. We then generalize to a family of instances showing that Pareto optimal $α$-EFX allocations may not exist for any $α> 2/3$.
☆ Cycle structure of best-response dynamics in random bimatrix games
Georgios Nikolaos Karelas, Gábor Lugosi, Rui-Ray Zhang
We study the best-response dynamics in games with random payoffs. We consider two-player bimatrix games, with $n$ strategies each. We assume that payoffs come from a continuous distribution, and study the best-response dynamics of these games, after imposing some structure on their payoff matrices. In particular, we focus on symmetric games, antisymmetric games, common-interest games, zero-sum games, and games with independent payoffs. When two players take turns in playing the best response to the opponent's action, they eventually end up cycling through the same sequence of actions. The main focus of the paper is the cycle structure of large random games. In particular, we study the number of cycles, the number of cycles of a certain length, the length of the longest cycle, and related quantities. We show that the structure of the game has an important impact on the typical cycle structure. Our arguments are based on a representation of the best-response dynamics of these games as directed bipartite graphs, and on the cycle structure that arises in them.
☆ Correlated Quantal Response Equilibrium: A New Equilibrium Notion for Human-AI Strategic Interactions
Zehao Zhao, Rahul Jain, Vijay Subramanian
The modeling of the behavior of agents in strategic environments and the prediction of the resulting outcomes has long been a challenging problem; this has been the focus of game theory. The introduction of AI agents as human-aids or as sole decision-makers expands the underlying question: Can we model behavior and predict outcomes of strategic games that involve a mix of AI agents and human players? As an initial answer, we propose Correlated Quantal Response Equilibrium (CQRE) that combines and generalizes classical solution concepts such as Quantal Response Equilibrium and Correlated Equilibrium. We answer questions of existence and propose a method for computing the CQRE that is a best fit to a given joint action distribution. We demonstrate the empirical effectiveness of CQRE predictions using a diverse collection of complex general-sum games, including high-rank and large-action two-player games, challenging multiplayer games, and a large-scale extension of the Selten--Chmura setting to AI--AI and human--AI play.
♻ ☆ On Sex, Evolution, and the Multiplicative Weights Update Algorithm AAMAS-2015
Reshef Meir, David Parkes
We consider a recent innovative theory by Chastain et al. on the role of sex in evolution [PNAS'14]. In short, the theory suggests that the evolutionary process of gene recombination implements the celebrated multiplicative weights updates algorithm (MWUA). They prove that the population dynamics induced by sexual reproduction can be precisely modeled by genes that use MWUA as their learning strategy in a particular coordination game. The result holds in the environments of \emph{weak selection}, under the assumption that the population frequencies remain a product distribution. We revisit the theory, eliminating both the requirement of weak selection and any assumption on the distribution of the population. Removing the assumption of product distributions is crucial, since as we show, this assumption is inconsistent with the population dynamics. We show that the marginal allele distributions induced by the population dynamics precisely match the marginals induced by a multiplicative weights update algorithm in this general setting, thereby affirming and substantially generalizing these earlier results. We further revise the implications for convergence and utility or fitness guarantees in coordination games. In contrast to the claim of Chastain et al.[PNAS'14], we conclude that the sexual evolutionary dynamics does not entail any property of the population distribution, beyond those already implied by convergence.
comment: full version of a paper accepted to AAMAS-2015
♻ ☆ AI-driven Prices for Externalities and Sustainability in Production Markets AAMAS 2023
Panayiotis Danassis, Aris Filos-Ratsikas, Haipeng Chen, Milind Tambe, Boi Faltings
Traditional competitive markets do not account for negative externalities; indirect costs that some participants impose on others, such as the cost of over-appropriating a common-pool resource (which diminishes future stock, and thus harvest, for everyone). Quantifying appropriate interventions to market prices has proven to be quite challenging. We propose a practical approach to computing market prices and allocations via a deep reinforcement learning policymaker agent, operating in an environment of other learning agents. Our policymaker allows us to tune the prices with regard to diverse objectives such as sustainability and resource wastefulness, fairness, buyers' and sellers' welfare, etc. As a highlight of our findings, our policymaker is significantly more successful in maintaining resource sustainability, compared to the market equilibrium outcome, in scarce resource environments.
comment: A preliminary version was accepted to the 22nd International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems (AAMAS 2023). This full version has been accepted at the journal of Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (Volume 40, article number 46, 2026)
♻ ☆ Learning to Allocate Resources with Censored Feedback
Giovanni Montanari, Côme Fiegel, Corentin Pla, Aadirupa Saha, Vianney Perchet
We study an online resource allocation problem in which at each round, a budget $B$ must be allocated across $K$ arms under censored feedback. An arm yields a reward if and only if two conditions are satisfied: (i) the arm is activated according to an arm-specific Bernoulli random variable with unknown parameter, and (ii) the allocated budget exceeds a random threshold drawn from a parametric distribution with unknown parameter. Over $T$ rounds, the learner must jointly estimate the unknown parameters and allocate the budget so as to maximize cumulative reward facing the exploration--exploitation trade-off. We prove a worst-case regret lower bound $Ω(\sqrt{T})$ for the general model, even with known uniform threshold distributions. We then propose RA-UCB, an optimistic algorithm that leverages non-trivial parameter estimation and confidence bounds. When the budget $B$ is known at the beginning of each round, RA-UCB achieves a regret bound of order $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$, and even $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{poly}\text{-}\log T)$ under stronger assumptions. As for unknown, round dependent budget, we introduce \texttt{MG-UCB}, which allows within-round switching and infinitesimal allocations, and matches the regret guarantees of RA-UCB. We then validate our theoretical results through experiments on real-world datasets.
♻ ☆ Moment Ambiguity and the Limits of Robust Stochastic Optimization
Andrés Cristi, Matteo Russo, Jiechen Zhang
We study fundamental information-theoretic limits of robust stochastic optimization when the distribution is known only through its exact moment sequence. We develop a unified framework that produces families of distinct distributions sharing all moments yet inducing radically different optimal decisions, thereby establishing strong impossibility results for a range of decision problems under moment ambiguity. Our binary and $N$-way moment-matching constructions separate quantiles, threshold regions, and online selection opportunities while preserving every moment. For the newsvendor problem, moment equivalence causes quantile ambiguity, inducing any fixed or randomized order quantity to fail arbitrarily badly. For revenue maximization, no deterministic or randomized posted pricing scheme can secure a nontrivial approximation relative to the full-information benchmark. For the secretary problem with cardinal observations, the optimal robust success probability under exact moment disclosure is the classical finite-horizon value $s_m$, even for i.i.d. observations. This value converges to $1/e$, compared with the full-information limit of approximately $0.5801$ due to Gilbert and Mosteller (J. Am. Stat. Assoc., 1966). We also recover and expand upon the recent impossibility result of Correa et al. (STOC, 2026) for prophet inequalities with moment knowledge. For every fixed $r\ge1$, exact moment knowledge can yield at best a $Θ(1/\log m)$ competitive ratio, even when competing against relaxed benchmarks based on expected $r$-th order statistics or when the algorithm is allowed to select $r$ items.
♻ ☆ Connecting Strategy Improvement, the Simplex Algorithm and Lopsidedness
Matthew Maat
The strategy improvement algorithm for mean payoff games and parity games is a local improvement algorithm, just like the simplex algorithm for linear programs. Their similarity has turned out very useful: many lower bounds on running time for the simplex algorithm have been created, by first constructing lower bounds for strategy improvement in a game, and then transforming these into a linear program. However, earlier connections between these algorithms required constructing an intermediate Markov decision process, which is not always possible. We prove a formal, direct connection between the two algorithms, showing that many variants of strategy improvement for parity and mean payoff games are truly an instance of the simplex algorithm, under mild nondegeneracy assumptions. The linear programming formulation of these games leads to what we call hypercubelike polyhedra. These polyhedra allow us to show combinatorial properties of various games on graphs. In particular, we show a connection between strategy sets of games and lopsided sets.
comment: Version 2: typos corrected, simplified proofs in section 4 and more polished in general
♻ ☆ Fixed Sets and the Hardness of Computing Correlated Equilibria
Ioannis Anagnostides, Constantinos Daskalakis, Gabriele Farina, Noah Golowich, Tuomas Sandholm, Brian Hu Zhang
We show that computing an approximate correlated equilibrium of a polytope game is PPAD-complete, and thus polynomial-time equivalent to finding a Nash equilibrium. This challenges the conventional view in game theory that correlated equilibria are more tractable objects than Nash equilibria. From a conceptual standpoint, we connect correlated equilibria to a natural generalization of fixed points, which we call fixed sets. A fixed set of a continuous function $f$ is a nonempty finite set $S$ such that $S \subseteq \operatorname{conv} f(S)$. Our main technical contribution is to prove that computing a fixed set is PPAD-hard even at inverse polynomial precision.
comment: V2 adjusted cross-reference labels; no changes to the technical content
♻ ☆ Deterministic algorithms for inhomogeneous Bernoulli trials: Shapley value of network devices
Jesse D Wei, Guo Wei
Suppose that $n$ computer devices are to be connected to a network via inhomogeneous Bernoulli trials. The Shapley value of a device quantifies how much the network's value increases due to the participation of that device. Characteristic functions of such games are naturally taken as the belief function (containment function) and Choquet capacity (hitting probability) of a random set (random network of devices). Traditionally, the Shapley value is either calculated as the expected marginal contribution over all possible coalitions (subnetworks), which results in exponential computational complexity, or approximated by the Monte Carlo sampling technique, where the performance is highly dependent on the stochastic sampling process. The purpose of this study is to design deterministic algorithms for games formulated via inhomogeneous Bernoulli trials that approximate the Shapley value in linear or quadratic time, with rigorous error analysis (Sections 3 and 4). Additionally, we provide a review of relevant literature on existing calculation methods in Remark 3.1 and Appendix I. A further goal is to supplement Shapley's original proof by deriving the Shapley value formula using a rigorous approach based on definite integrals and combinatorial analysis. This method explicitly highlights the roles of the Binomial Theorem and the Beta function in the proof, addressing a gap in Shapley's work (Appendix II).
comment: 27 pages
♻ ☆ Allocating Indivisible Goods to Strategic Agents: Pure Nash Equilibria and Fairness
Georgios Amanatidis, Georgios Birmpas, Federico Fusco, Philip Lazos, Stefano Leonardi, Rebecca Reiffenhäuser
We consider the problem of fairly allocating a set of indivisible goods to a set of strategic agents with additive valuation functions. We assume no monetary transfers and, therefore, a mechanism in our setting is an algorithm that takes as input the reported -- rather than the true -- values of the agents. Our main goal is to explore whether there exist mechanisms that have pure Nash equilibria for every instance and, at the same time, provide fairness guarantees for the allocations that correspond to these equilibria. We focus on two relaxations of envy-freeness, namely envy-freeness up to one good (EF1), and envy-freeness up to any good (EFX), and we positively answer the above question. In particular, we study two algorithms that are known to produce such allocations in the non-strategic setting: Round-Robin (EF1 allocations for any number of agents) and a cut-and-choose algorithm of Plaut and Roughgarden [SIAM Journal of Discrete Mathematics, 2020] (EFX allocations for two agents). For Round-Robin we show that all of its pure Nash equilibria induce allocations that are EF1 with respect to the underlying true values, while for the algorithm of Plaut and Roughgarden we show that the corresponding allocations not only are EFX but also satisfy maximin share fairness, something that is not true for this algorithm in the non-strategic setting! Further, we show that a weaker version of the latter result holds for any mechanism for two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria which all induce EFX allocations.
comment: The claim that every pure Nash equilibrium of Round-Robin is EF1 (Theorem 3.3 here; Theorem 3 in the conference version and Theorem 4 in the journal version) is incorrect; the gap is in the proof of Lemma 3.5 (inequality (2)). A counterexample and corrected guarantees are given in arXiv:2610.23686. The remaining results are not affected
♻ ☆ Blockchain Monetary Policy, Strategic Participation, and the Dynamics of Decentralization
Diodato Ferraioli, Paolo Penna, Manvir Schneider, Carmine Ventre
Blockchain systems must navigate a fundamental tradeoff between rewarding capable participants for performance and preserving a sufficiently decentralized distribution of stake. We study this tradeoff through algorithmic reward policies in dynamic blockchain environments with publicly known capability types and evolving token stakes. We analyze two settings. First, under full participation, we study virtual-stake policies that combine type and stake in winner selection. We show that fixed virtual-stake rules exhibit strong path dependence, and that this limitation extends to broader winner-selection rules based on virtual stake; when the type weight varies over time, the winner distribution asymptotically approaches either stake-proportional or type-proportional selection. Second, we study a repeated participation game in which agents may abstain, rewards update stake, and token value depends on the decentralization of the participating stake. We characterize stage equilibria under myopic behavior. In this environment, strongly performance-favoring winner-take-most policies can drive the system to minimum decentralization under myopic play. We then identify policies that preserve participation or decentralization only by departing from strict performance-first reward design. In particular, our analysis identifies three benchmarks: policies that spread winner eligibility across the top-$k$ types, policies that simulate lookahead, and broad-sharing reward rules. Each mitigates failures of performance-first designs with different tradeoffs in participation, robustness, and performance priority. Overall, our results suggest that winner selection alone does not robustly resolve the capability-stake tradeoff: sustaining decentralization requires reward rules that react explicitly to concentration, even when this entails sacrificing some immediate performance advantage.
♻ ☆ Disjoint Stable Matchings in Linear Time
Aadityan Ganesh, Vishwa Prakash HV, Prajakta Nimbhorkar, Geevarghese Philip
We show that given a SM instance G as input we can find a largest collection of pairwise edge-disjoint stable matchings of G in time linear in the input size. This extends two classical results: 1. The Gale-Shapley algorithm, which can find at most two ("extreme") pairwise edge-disjoint stable matchings of G in linear time, and 2. The polynomial-time algorithm for finding a largest collection of pairwise edge-disjoint perfect matchings (without the stability requirement) in a bipartite graph, obtained by combining König's characterization with Tutte's f-factor algorithm. Moreover, we also give an algorithm to enumerate all maximum-length chains of disjoint stable matchings in the lattice of stable matchings of a given instance. This algorithm takes time polynomial in the input size for enumerating each chain. We also derive the expected number of such chains in a random instance of Stable Matching. For the Stable Roomates problem, we show that determining if a given instance admits at most two disjoint stable matchings or three disjoint stable matchings is NP-complete.
comment: Extended to include results on Stable Roommates problem. Published WG 2021
♻ ☆ RuleSmith: Multi-Agent LLMs for Automated Game Balancing NeurIPS 2026
Ziyao Zeng, Hao Wang, Chen Liu, Youheng Yao, Jingcheng Ni, Tianyu Liu, Xiatao Sun, Fengyu Yang, Chenyu You, Xiaofeng Liu, Daniel Rakita, Ronald R. Coifman, Yuval Kluger, Zhiwen Fan
Game balancing is a longstanding challenge requiring repeated playtesting, expert intuition, and extensive manual tuning. We introduce RuleSmith, a framework that couples multi-agent LLM self-play with surrogate-based optimization over a parameterized rule space. As a proof of concept, we build CivMini, a simplified civilization-style game with two asymmetric factions governed by 12 tunable parameters. LLM agents interpret textual rulebooks and game states to propose actions that are validated by the game engine, yielding noisy estimates of faction win rates. Our primary implementation uses Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization with Expected-Improvement-based adaptive sampling to allocate more evaluation games to promising candidates. RuleSmith consistently finds near-balanced configurations: three independent optimization runs reach near-even empirical win rates in independent 200- and 300-game evaluations, and additional experiments with NTBEA and TPE show that the same self-play interface supports different search components. Cross-model evaluations and small human studies provide preliminary evidence of transfer across player populations. RuleSmith produces interpretable numerical rule adjustments without task-specific policy training. Project and code: https://adonis-galaxy.github.io/RuleSmith-website/

Information Retrieval
☆ HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning
Sudipta Paul, Pengrui Quan, Aounon Kumar, Nicholas Tzou, Vivek Kulkarni, Srinivas Chappidi
Harness optimization, which improves an agent's prompts, tools, and workflows, is an increasingly effective way to enhance agents built on frozen or closed-source LLMs. Leading approaches such as the Darwin--Godel Machine and the Huxley--Godel Machine (HGM) rely on recursive self-improvement and were developed mainly for coding, where the competence needed to improve the agent coincides with the competence being improved. Planning tasks, in which an agent must produce a sequence of tool calls that jointly satisfies interacting constraints, break this alignment. There, open-ended self-modification repeatedly explores ineffective changes and consumes substantial evaluation budgets. We introduce HGM-Dual, a diagnostic-guided framework for budget-efficient harness evolution for planning agents. First, HGM-Dual represents agent evolution as lineage-aware context. This context records what each ancestor changed, which behaviors improved or regressed, and which modifications were ineffective, giving the editor explicit edit-outcome attribution instead of an unstructured archive of past agents. Second, HGM-Dual introduces error-conditioned dual-path child generation. For each selected parent, it generates a general child that preserves open-ended exploration and specialized children that target the harness components most likely responsible for the parent's highest-ranked constraint violations. HGM-Dual outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 14.45% relative improvement in case accuracy while matching HGM variants' final performance with 2x-4x fewer evaluation budget.
☆ Probing Spatial and Spectral Grounding in EEG Foundation Models
Kleanthis Avramidis, Ivan Tashev, Dimitra Emmanouilidou
EEG foundation models are advancing at an unprecedented pace, yet their evaluation is driven by downstream accuracy, which reveals little about whether their predictions rely on physiologically interpretable signal structure. We introduce a set of perturbation probes in two grounding axes: spatial grounding in channel identity and topographic locality, and spectral grounding in oscillatory content and waveform morphology. We apply these probes to five published EEG foundation models across motor-imagery and seizure recordings. Our experiments reveal differences in both representational sensitivity and downstream reliance. Electrode identity may be encoded without influencing downstream classification: permuting LaBraM's positional codes heavily displaced its embeddings yet reduced motor-imagery accuracy by only 1.2 points, while spectral details may be discriminable without producing specific responses to simulated clinical markers, as only REVE exceeded a spectral baseline on this task. These dissociations are hidden in common benchmarks, demonstrating how grounding probes can complement performance-based evaluation by revealing what EEG foundation models encode and what their predictions depend on.

☆ BrainCodes: A Lightweight EEG Foundation Model over Discrete Neural Codes
Kleanthis Avramidis, Ivan Tashev, Dimitra Emmanouilidou
Recent electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models increasingly emphasize model scale, potentially limiting their deployment on resource-constrained devices and in everyday environments. We argue that transferable EEG features can instead be learned with a compact architecture and introduce BrainCodes, a lightweight foundation model pretrained through self-supervised learning on more than 800 hours of recordings from over 1,000 participants. Our architecture combines a quantization-based neural tokenizer with a spatiotemporal encoder that supports arbitrary electrode configurations. The pretraining objective explicitly encourages representations that capture spatial connectivity through channel positional encoding, and sensitivity to narrowband neural oscillations through an auxiliary training objective. Our model matches or surpasses the state of the art across diverse neurophysiological monitoring tasks, including sleep staging, attention assessment, and cognitive load estimation. BrainCodes transfers effectively to low-resource wearable devices while using up to 97% fewer trainable parameters than comparable architectures. Beyond predictive accuracy, our evaluation framework characterizes the geometry and invariances of learned EEG representations across measurable spatial, temporal, and spectral signal properties.
comment: Preprint. Under review
☆ Gate Initialisation versus Recurrent Dropout and Zoneout in Learning Long Dependencies: A Controlled Study of LSTM and GRU Networks on Synthetic Tasks
Oleksandr Kholodniak, Oleksandr Prokhorov
Dropout and zoneout are routinely added to long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU) networks, but, to our knowledge, their placements have not been crossed with gate initialisation in a factorial design, and it is not known whether early gradient propagation tells which runs will learn long dependencies. We trained one-layer LSTMs and GRUs on the adding problem and on delayed recall in a factorial grid of 720 runs, crossing conventional and chrono gate initialisation with up to six recurrent regulariser placements at one rate each, with pre-specified follow-ups, and recorded how sensitive the final hidden state was to the input at every lag. Because both tasks supply fresh or exhaustive training data, the study measures the regularisers' effects on optimisation and does not assess generalisation from a finite training set. At lengths chosen to make conventional initialisation difficult, all 360 chrono-initialised runs reached the validation criterion within 5000 updates, as did 119 of 120 unregularised runs with a horizon about four times too short or too long, whereas conventionally initialised networks learned slowly or did not reach the criterion within the budget at the longer lengths. Under conventional initialisation, dropout generally delayed learning and zoneout helped only in some conditions. The early input sensitivity added little to predicting which conditions learn once the early validation loss was modelled per task, architecture and initialisation. Within conditions, a flatter early decay went with the seeds that learned, but in a pre-specified test the association was modest (concordance 0.61), condition-dependent and not robust to resampling seeds. The results support chrono initialisation, even with a rough horizon, on such tasks.

♻ ☆ Beyond Accuracy: Measuring Logical Compliance of Predictive Models
Guillaume Olivier Delplanque, Pierre Genevès, Nabil Layaïda
Machine learning models are predominantly evaluated through predictive performance metrics such as ranking quality, prediction error, or classification accuracy. While these metrics effectively quantify how closely predictions match the ground truth, they do not assess whether model outputs respect predefined logical or domain-specific constraints. In high-stakes applications, including healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, logical consistency can be as critical as predictive accuracy, yet no standard metric captures this dimension. We introduce the Rule Violation Score (RVS), a complementary evaluation metric that quantifies the extent to which a predictive model respects a given set of logical rules, independently of predictive accuracy. RVS treats hard rules (strict constraints) and soft rules (statistical regularities) differently, can be evaluated on any dataset and on any predictive model expressed over a relational vocabulary, and can be computed using SQL queries that are automatically generated for Horn rules. Beyond evaluating models, RVS can also evaluate the logical consistency of training datasets and help identify poorly defined rules. We evaluate RVS on three benchmarks covering knowledge graph link prediction and relational regression, including rule-based, embedding-based, and neuro-symbolic predictive models. Our results demonstrate that two models achieving comparable predictive accuracy can exhibit substantially different levels of logical compliance, revealing differences in model behavior that standard metrics fail to capture.
♻ ☆ Understanding Transformer-Based Vision Models via Modular Feature Inversion
Jan Rathjens, Shirin Reyhanian, David Kappel, Laurenz Wiskott
Understanding the internal mechanisms of deep neural networks remains a central challenge in machine learning. In computer vision, one promising yet only preliminarily explored approach is feature inversion via inverse networks, which reconstructs images from intermediate representations using trained inverse networks. In this study, we revisit feature inversion via inverse networks, introducing a novel, modular variant that enables a computationally more efficient application of the technique while, in some cases, producing semantically more coherent image reconstructions. We apply our method to large-scale transformer-based vision models, specifically Detection Transformer, Vision Transformer, Swin Transformer, and Data-Efficient Image Transformer, analyzing the resulting reconstructions across network depth. Our main analysis compares Detection Transformer and Vision Transformer, which exhibit the most informative differences among the evaluated architectures. At the same time, results for Swin Transformer and Data-Efficient Image Transformer support the broader applicability of our framework. Our findings reveal gradual representational changes across transformer layers as a shared characteristic of Detection Transformer and Vision Transformer, as well as systematic differences in how they preserve contextual shape and fine-grained image details, and in their robustness to color perturbations. These findings deepen understanding of transformer-based vision models and demonstrate the utility of modular feature inversion as an interpretability tool.

♻ ☆ Quality-Diversity Red-Teaming: Automated Generation of High-Quality and Diverse Attackers for Large Language Models
Ren-Jian Wang, Ke Xue, Zeyu Qin, Ziniu Li, Sheng Tang, Hao-Tian Li, Shengcai Liu, Zhi Yu, Yuanpeng Tan, Chao Qian
Ensuring the safety and robustness of large language models (LLMs) is a fundamental challenge and a critical prerequisite for the responsible deployment of artificial intelligence. Red-teaming, a systematic framework to identify adversarial prompts that elicit harmful responses from target LLMs, has emerged as a crucial safety evaluation paradigm. Within this framework, the diversity of adversarial prompts is critical for a comprehensive safety assessment. However, previous red-teaming approaches often pursue diversity through simplistic metrics such as word frequency or sentence embedding similarity, which may not capture meaningful variation in attack strategies. In addition, the common practice of training a single attacker model restricts coverage across all potential attack styles and risk categories. This paper introduces Quality-Diversity Red-Teaming (QDRT), a new framework designed to address these limitations. QDRT achieves goal-driven diversity through behavior-conditioned training and implements a behavioral replay buffer in an open-ended manner. In addition, it trains multiple specialized attackers capable of generating high-quality attacks across diverse styles and risk categories. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates that QDRT generates attacks that are both more diverse and more effective against a wide range of target LLMs, including open-source models \texttt{GPT-2}, \texttt{Llama-3}, \texttt{Gemma-2}, \texttt{Qwen2.5}, and commercial models \texttt{GPT-4.1} and \texttt{GPT-5-Chat}. This work advances the field of LLM safety by providing a systematic and effective approach to automated red-teaming, ultimately supporting the responsible deployment of LLMs. Our code is available at https://github.com/lamda-bbo/QDRT.

Computer Science and Game Theory
☆ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel? What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets
Hieu Tran, Hong Yu
Evaluations of large language model (LLM) agents report that pricing agents collude at others' expense. Yet collusion is defined by enforcement: a cartel, in which competitors share monopoly profits, holds only if a member who cheats is punished. We introduce an audit that tests enforcement by forcing a member to cheat in counterfactual copies of a market, and use it to study what reinforcement learning (RL) teaches agents in pricing and trading. Small LLMs trained by RL learn what their training rivals reward, but only what they readily try. In self-play, they learn fixed rules ignoring their rivals; against a punishing rival, to be deterred; against a cheating rival, to match its cuts, never the costly price war that would deter it, which they rarely try. A war forced into training is learned, but mostly only where it was forced. Against their own copies, deterred and matching agents can earn the same cartel profits, but only matching ones can enforce them, and then thinly: as a by-product and only against large cuts. Q-learners enforce collusion only in pricing. Prompted LLMs reach cartel-like outcomes mostly through rules that ignore the market. Outcome measures cannot tell these cases apart; the audit can.

☆ Exact Envy-Free Cake Cutting with Polynomial Expected Queries
Simon Mackenzie, Mashbat Suzuki
Envy-free cake cutting asks how to divide a resource so that no agent prefers another agent's share. Finding such a division with few queries about preferences has been a longstanding challenge. Aziz and Mackenzie gave the first query bound depending only on the number $n$ of agents: a tower of six $n$'s. Subsequent improvements culminated in Ye and Bai's single-exponential bound of $n^{O(1)}2^n$. A large gap remains between this deterministic upper bound and Procaccia's general lower bound of $Ω(n^2)$. Whether polynomially many queries suffice is a central open question in fair division. We show that a polynomial expected query bound is possible. Our randomised protocol uses only independent, uniformly sampled points from the cake as its source of randomness. For every profile of $n$ agents with nonnegative, additive, nonatomic valuations, the protocol has the following guarantees: (1) It terminates with probability one. (2) Every allocation it returns is complete and exactly envy-free. (3) Its expected number of Robertson-Webb queries is $\widetilde{O}(n^{30})$. The expectation is taken solely over the protocol's random choices, with no distributional assumptions on preferences.

☆ Subjective Valuations Make It Hard to be Fair: The Complexity of Resource Allocation to Groups of Agents
Argyrios Deligkas, Eduard Eiben, Robert Ganian, Tiger-Lily Goldsmith, Marlene Gründel, Simon Wietheger
We study the parameterized complexity of finding an EF1 allocation of indivisible items in the group-sharing setting, which has received increasing attention in recent years. There, items are not allocated to individual agents but rather to one of two (or possibly more) groups, and agents within that group all share the assigned items. We consider both the "fixed" (EF1-Fix) and "variable" (EF1-Var) group cases, where in the former the assignments of agents to groups are prescribed. While both are NP-hard in the classical sense, we show that their algorithmic behavior differs significantly from the parameterized perspective. As our main results, we: (1) prove that both cases are NP-hard even when the number of agents is a small constant; (2) circumvent this hardness by establishing fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Var w.r.t. the number of "subjective" items, that is, items which are viewed as chores or goods by different agents---but rule out an analogous result for EF1-Fix; and (3) establish fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Fix w.r.t. the number of item types, but link the existence of an analogous fixed-parameter algorithm for EF1-Var to a fundamental open question in the setting of Integer Linear Programming.
♻ ☆ Falsification-proof non-market allocation mechanisms
Eduardo Perez-Richet, Vasiliki Skreta
Relying on manipulable characteristics to target the allocation of resources is fraught with difficulties. Naively optimal rules lead to falsification and allocative inefficiency. Optimizing the rule for allocative efficiency while accounting for falsification typically induces falsification, at a heavy cost to the agents. Moreover, falsification generates negative externalities. We characterize optimal falsification-proof rules under a broad range of falsification technologies. We also provide an honesty condition under which they solve the unconstrained problem of a planner who maximizes a weighted sum of allocative surplus and agents' welfare.

We prove an $Ω(q/\log q)$ lower bound on the competitive ratio. Together with the known $O(q)$ upper bounds, this resolves, up to a logarithmic factor, the optimal dependence on $q$, an open question posed by Correa, Cristi, Fielbaum, Pollner, and Weinberg (IPCO 2022) and Saxena, Velusamy, and Weinberg (ITCS 2023). Our construction also yields an $Ω(d/\log d)$ lower bound for $d$-single-minded auctions, where buyers request fixed bundles of at most $d$ unit-capacity items. Our construction and analysis build on the big-decisions-first framework of Rubinstein and Singla (STOC 2026). Previous lower bounds for this problem hold even for i.i.d. Bernoulli values, whereas our instance uses nonidentical distributions. For i.i.d. Bernoulli values, we prove a $q^{1-o(1)}$ lower bound, improving the previous $q^{1/2+Ω(1/\log\log q)}$ of Saxena, Velusamy, and Weinber (ITCS 2023). To this end, we construct $p^p$ pairwise qualitatively independent partitions into $p$ blocks on a ground set of only $p^{2+o(1)}$ points.
♻ ☆ Continuation-Adjusted Full-Support Indifference in a Feedback Stackelberg Attacker--Defender Attrition Game
Azhar Iqbal, James M. Chappell, Derek Abbott
Successful attacks that remove assets break two familiar static regularities: coverage need not deter attack, and the defender need not push coverage until its budget or an individual target saturates. We analyse a finite-horizon attacker--defender attrition game under a stagewise feedback-recommitment strong Stackelberg equilibrium. Our central result is a continuation adjustment that converts each state--period node into a static security game with shifted payoffs. At feasible full-support nodes, coverage remains indexed by one scalar attacker value, so backward induction uses scalar interval and endpoint calculations; boundary-support nodes require conditional linear programmes. Continuation losses can reverse an attacker's coverage swing, making a covered asset more attractive because it survives for later attacks. A three-asset, two-period instance is solved globally for every discount factor. It exhibits an exact singular threshold at which the optimal set expands, the selected policy jumps, and the defender abandons a previously protected asset and leaves budget unused with no target saturated, although both players' values remain continuous.

♻ ☆ A Complete Characterization of Convexity in Flow Games
Han Xiao, Luying Zhang, Qizhi Fang
Flow games coincide precisely with non-negative totally balanced games. We give a complete characterization of convexity for flow games with one arc per player. We prove that such a game is convex if and only if all simple source-to-sink paths can simultaneously carry their full path capacities. Equivalently, after deleting null arcs, the topology is a funnel network, and every arc can meet the combined demand of the paths through it. We provide polyhedral characterizations of convexity. In primal form, the game is convex if and only if the path-flow polytope is a box, allowing each path flow to vary independently up to its capacity. In dual form, convexity is equivalent to the existence of a minimum source-to-sink cut consisting entirely of private arcs. An arc is private if it belongs to exactly one simple source-to-sink path. We also give a polynomial-time algorithm that tests whether a given flow game is convex.

☆ Unit-Aware Differentially Private Quantum Machine Learning for Clinical and Wearable Health Data
Md Khalid Syfullah, Alvi Ataur Khalil
Clinical registries and wearable sensors support early health-risk assessment, yet models trained on these records may leak sensitive information when released. Differential privacy (DP) bounds this leakage by injecting noise whose total magnitude grows with the number of trainable parameters, a cost especially severe for small health cohorts. This motivates parameter efficient models including quantum machine learning (QML), whose variational circuits can represent complex decision boundaries with few trainable parameters. It raises a question: at matched input dimensionality and privacy budget, does a quantum model retain more utility than a classical one? We investigate this question on three clinical cohorts and one wearable cohort, treating each clinical record or participant as a privacy unit. We compare capacity-matched quantum, multilayer perceptron, and logistic regression models across five privacy budgets and five seeds. The quantum model leads on three clinical cohorts by up to 0.104 ROC AUC averaged across budgets; however, trails on the wearable cohort, where the small number of participants requires substantial noise. No difference survives Holm correction across 24 tests, so these results indicate a trend rather than a quantum advantage. An analytic gradient bound shows that lower clipping thresholds can improve utility by reducing noise despite clipping bias. Finally, an experiment on IBM quantum computer (ibm_fez, a 156-qubit superconducting processor) using eight fixed test cases yields mean absolute probability errors of 0.046 (private) and 0.063 (non-private) relative to simulation, supporting the feasibility of inference on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/DP-QML-Health.
☆ Multi-Objective Evolutionary Semi-Supervised Learning for Resource-Aware Smart City Classification SC
Francisco José Sedeño, Jamal Toutouh
Smart-city applications often combine scarce labeled data with abundant unlabeled observations. Semi-supervised learning (SSL) exploits both labeled and unlabeled data to improve classification under limited supervision. This article presents MOEA-SSL, a multi-objective evolutionary approach for lightweight semi-supervised tabular classification that jointly optimizes predictive quality and feature usage. Experimental evaluation on three Smart City classification datasets, considering 1\%, 5\%, and 10\% labeled data, shows that MOEA-SSL achieves competitive predictive performance compared with established lightweight SSL methods while significantly reducing feature usage relative to EA-SSL in all evaluated conditions. The computed Pareto fronts also provide lower-feature-use alternatives with limited degradation in classification performance.

♻ ☆ Taskonomy: Disentangling Task Transfer Learning CVPR 2018
Amir Zamir, Alexander Sax, William Shen, Leonidas Guibas, Jitendra Malik, Silvio Savarese
Do visual tasks have a relationship, or are they unrelated? For instance, could having surface normals simplify estimating the depth of an image? Intuition answers these questions positively, implying existence of a structure among visual tasks. Knowing this structure has notable values; it is the concept underlying transfer learning and provides a principled way for identifying redundancies across tasks, e.g., to seamlessly reuse supervision among related tasks or solve many tasks in one system without piling up the complexity. We proposes a fully computational approach for modeling the structure of space of visual tasks. This is done via finding (first and higher-order) transfer learning dependencies across a dictionary of twenty six 2D, 2.5D, 3D, and semantic tasks in a latent space. The product is a computational taxonomic map for task transfer learning. We study the consequences of this structure, e.g. nontrivial emerged relationships, and exploit them to reduce the demand for labeled data. For example, we show that the total number of labeled datapoints needed for solving a set of 10 tasks can be reduced by roughly 2/3 (compared to training independently) while keeping the performance nearly the same. We provide a set of tools for computing and probing this taxonomical structure including a solver that users can employ to devise efficient supervision policies for their use cases.

♻ ☆ Compute-Optimal Scaling Laws for Spiking Language Models NeurIPS 2026
Dan Saunders, Benjamin Ren, Catherine He
Spiking neural networks target energy-efficient language modeling through sparse, binary activations, but the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff of spiking language models is uncharacterized at scale. We present the first Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP scaling study of a spiking language model, sweeping SpikeGPT-family models (RWKV backbone) from width 384 to 1536 across compute budgets from $3\times10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ FLOPs on FineWeb-EDU. We report two findings. First, the compute-optimal frontier is $N_{opt} \propto C^{0.56}$, close to the 0.50 that Hoffmann et al. report for dense Transformers, so spiking does not change how parameters and data should be traded off under a compute budget. Second, against non-spiking RWKV and Transformer baselines trained the same way, the loss gap splits into a backbone cost of about 0.16 nats that does not change with compute and a spiking cost that falls steadily with compute, from 0.34 to 0.23 nats over our range. These results give the first compute-optimal recipe for spiking language models and quantify the accuracy cost of their sparsity.

♻ ☆ Predator-Prey Model: Driven Hunt for Accelerated Grokking
I. A. Lopatin, S. V. Kozyrev, A. N. Pechen
A machine learning method is proposed using two agents (representing two coupled replicas of the model parameters) that simulate the biological behavior of a predator and a prey. In this method, the two agents interact with each other via a pair of potentials that simulate the dynamics when the predator chases the prey while the prey runs away from the predator - to perform an optimization on the landscape. This method allows, for optimization landscapes with narrow ravines with gentle slope or even flat bottoms, to avoid optimization getting stuck in a ravine. For some examples of grokking (i.e., delayed generalization) problems we show that this method allows for achieving up to a hundred times faster learning in gradient evaluations and up to 60 times in the wall-clock time compared to the standard learning procedure.

♻ ☆ Differential Functionalism: Jacobians Shape the Structure of Phenomenal Experience
David Balduzzi
This paper investigates the hypothesis that the first-order structure of physical interactions (Jacobians) shapes the structure of phenomenal experience. Two measures of Jacobian structure are introduced: transparency, the effective rank, which counts the independent differences that make a difference; and integrity, the normalised algebraic connectivity, which measures how hard a system is to split. Applied to a series of worked examples, the framework yields correlates of: (1) experiences that overlap without systems merging; (2) the boundaries of a system, which are selected by focus and limited by noise; (3) temporal thickness, the persistence of the past into the present, lengthened by a spread of timescales; (4) spatial structure under convolution, where unity at scale needs long-range connections; (5) the distinction between what is vivid and what is obscure, for errors and attention heads; (6) the incoherence of a randomly initialised network, as a structural model of James's "blooming, buzzing confusion"; (7) distinct versus confused ideas; (8) learning as accumulated experience; and, conjecturally, (9) the contrast between memory as duration in brains and as storage in computer hardware. The measures can be computed at scale in artificial networks and estimated from perturbational data in brains.

♻ ☆ One-shot learning of paired association navigation with biologically plausible schemas

After learning a multiple paired-association (MPA) navigation task, rodents can rapidly learn new cue-location associations after a single exposure, a phenomenon proposed to be facilitated by cognitive schemas. However, it remains unclear what schemas support this behavior and how they could be implemented in biological neural circuits. Here, we identify a set of schemas sufficient for gradual then one-shot paired-association navigation, and implement them in a fully neural agent using biologically plausible plasticity rules. The agent gradually acquires a low-dimensional spatial metric representation using a path-integration based temporal-difference error, enabling self-localization across different environments. It also contains a memory network that forms one-shot associations between sensory cues and goal locations, implemented using reward-modulated exploratory Hebbian (EH) plasticity. A third network performs vector subtraction between the agent's current and goal location to compute goal-directed actions. Supplementing these schemas with an actor-critic enables one-shot navigation past obstacles. Lastly, learning a working-memory gating mechanism using the temporal-difference error enables one-shot learning even with brief cue and distractor presentation. The model reproduces key behavioral features of rodent learning in the MPA task and generates testable predictions about the neural mechanisms underlying schema-based one-shot learning.

☆ A Spiking Ring-Attractor Architecture for Representation and Control of Revolute Robot Joints

Homeostatic regulation computes goal-state mismatch directly over these distributed representations, and opponent gain-modulated populations convert this mismatch into controlled phase shifts of the activity bump, implementing set-point regulation as motion on the ring. We show that the bump dynamics follow an SO(2) geometry, and that gain asymmetries induce a signed phase velocity on the ring. For multi-joint systems, we demonstrate that local ring-based Fourier features compose into product representations that linearly decode SO(3) orientations through forward kinematics. Experiments in NEST validate the full SO(2) regulation mechanism and the spiking product-feature decoder for lift, pitch, and yaw. Robot experiments on a Tiago arm show that decoded ring dynamics generate joint velocity commands, producing directed motion with joint-dependent accuracy. Together, these results establish a neuromorphic control framework in which representation, regulation, and action are unified within a ring-attractor substrate aligned with the geometry of revolute systems.

☆ Sector-Ring Linear Reservoirs: Sector-Wise Decay-Timescale Allocation With State Reuse Across Candidate Settings

In reservoir computing, performance depends on whether the fixed dynamics of the reservoir suit the task, and the appropriate memory length and frequency response differ across tasks. The reservoir settings are found by a search on each task, and driving the reservoir with the input and collecting its states for every candidate setting dominates the cost of the search. In a reservoir with a linear recurrence, the dynamics decompose into modes, one per eigenvalue, and the eigenvalue distribution becomes a design variable. We propose the Sector-Ring Linear Reservoir (SRLR), in which the eigenvalue angles are fixed at evenly spaced positions around a circle and one decay timescale, chosen from a few values, is assigned to each sector of consecutive angles. To keep the scale of each mode's state equal across candidates, the input weights are scaled using the power spectrum of the training input. To reduce the cost of the search, the states of the modes for each decay-timescale value are computed once and reused across candidates. On prediction and reconstruction benchmarks built from chaotic systems, the SRLR achieved, in all eight cases, a lower mean test error than a reference model in which all modes share one decay timescale, and was competitive with nonlinear echo state network and leaky-integrator echo state network baselines. The selected decay-timescale profiles changed with the prediction target and horizon. The state reuse reduced the number of computed mode trajectories in the search by 99.8% relative to per-candidate recomputation.

As neuromorphic systems scale to thousands of near-memory cores, aging-induced permanent faults in neuron-update datapaths become an important obstacle to long-term deployment. Existing online recovery methods typically retire a faulty core and migrate its neurons, along with their weights and membrane states, to healthy cores. This whole-core treatment incurs high recovery traffic and makes recovery depend on scarce destinations; at high utilization, there may be enough surviving compute capacity but insufficient free storage to copy the affected neuron context. This paper presents SpikeRelay, an online recovery framework for diagnosed compute-unit faults. Kargi Chauhan, Sadiba Nusrat Nur, Pratibha Revankar, Kyle Montgomery, Chenguang Wang
Agents that run for a long time have a memory problem, and it is not the one most systems optimize for. Storing every trace and retrieving the nearest neighbors works early and quietly stops working later: the store fills up with failures the agent then repeats, and with facts that were true fifty turns ago. RSPM (Recursive Self-Pruning Memory) borrows the fix biology already found. At intervals the agent sleeps. It clusters its recent failures, distills each cluster into a short rule, and deletes the raw episodes it just learned from. Rules decay unless something reinforces them, and rules that recur across many contexts get promoted into general ones. We tested this on three settings with little in common: a difficulty-calibrated SWE-bench simulation, temporal consistency across 12 conversational benchmarks, and long-horizon QA on LoCoMo-10. All three improve, by 9.1, 11.9, and 7.6 points respectively. More interestingly, the two studies that instrument the store itself converge on nearly the same operating point without being tuned toward it: roughly 93% fewer retry loops and roughly 30% fewer stored entries. That hints that knowing what to forget is a general property of agent memory rather than a benchmark-specific trick.

We identify a current-generated exact connection component that the tested instantaneous reconstruction and scalar local closure miss. Resetting this component at fixed density and Gauss-law curl changes the future density response within the chosen gauge and drift law and the small effect persists under numerical refinement. A signal-to-noise analysis gives the overlap with an unseen archetype in closed form: a majority-rule law in which an attention entropy replaces the dataset entropy. At high temperature the archetype is lost in the crosstalk; at low temperature the softmax freezes on the closest training example, as in a random energy model, and the layer memorizes. In between, in a window widening with the square root of the network size, the layer pools the examples of the correct class and retrieves the unseen archetype as well as their majority vote allows, at any fixed load. On structured datasets, such as MNIST and fashion-MNIST, the best accuracy lies beyond the freezing.

Fourth, an adaptive stagnation-aware Runge--Kutta correction is introduced to mitigate premature convergence. IWOO is evaluated on the IEEE CEC2019, CEC2022, and CEC2017 benchmark suites against representative and high-performing optimizers, with ablation studies assessing the contribution of each strategy. Within the representative algorithm group, IWOO achieves Friedman ranks of 1.8000, 1.5833, and 1.4483 on CEC2019, CEC2022, and CEC2017, respectively. Tests on six constrained engineering optimization problems further demonstrate its competitive accuracy, stability, and practical applicability.
♻ ☆ From anatomy to computation: axonal delay dispersion shifts neurons from event to sequence detection
Cheng Bi, Jipeng Sun
Cortical neurons fire sparsely -- often fewer than one spike per sensory window -- so a neuron's spike count in that window carries little information, and its spike timing can carry more. That conduction delays convert firing order into synchrony is long established. What governs which class of temporal feature a neuron detects -- one volley of coincident input, or two in a particular order -- has not been examined. We propose a delay-signature framework in which the axonal conduction delays converging on a dendritic branch or a small neuron's soma constitute a physical key: only input sequences whose spike-time differences the delays compensate arrive synchronously, and coincidence detection, a threshold on input summed within an inhibition-compressed window, converts that synchrony into an all-or-none output. First, in simulations of an integrator-neuron model, a single physical scalar -- the dispersion of the delay set -- moves a population from event to order-selective sequence detection. The transition is emergent under random delays and connectivity, and an exact calculation reproduces it: at narrow dispersion, sequence detectors do not exist, and the dispersion at which they overtake event detectors tracks the inter-event interval. This maps a computational distinction onto the anatomical one between myelinated and unmyelinated projections, making myelination a switch on what a neuron computes. Second, the same dispersion sets the code's limits: it bounds the longest codable interval and fixes an absolute timing tolerance of order a millisecond, the same at every dispersion. Third, that millisecond window and the conduction velocity of afferents inside cortex together set column diameter, and column anatomy predicts the window measured in mouse barrel cortex. One anatomically measurable parameter thus shapes what a neuron detects and sets the limits of what it can represent.

♻ ☆ Riding the Fixed-Point Curve: Image Classification in the Continuous Thought Machine NeurIPS 2026
Thomas Hannagan
The Continuous Thought Machine (CTM) is a recurrent network that attends to inputs and makes predictions based on the synchronization between its neurons. On tasks spanning many domains, it displays emergent thought processes that have not been explained. We report a number of findings about how the CTM classifies images, focusing on ImageNet. Thinking steps are attracting but strongly non-normal maps exhibiting balanced amplification (Murphy and Miller, 2009); while attraction is already present at CTM initialization, training highly promotes non-normality. By Banach's theorem, the neural state thus has a locally unique attracting fixed point, which moves at every step, and the thought trajectory is the curve these fixed points trace, followed one tick behind. Most of that curve's motion is shared across images, and visible as a previously reported traveling wave of activity across neurons. The attention schedule along the thought is largely generic: shuffling queries across images at every tick costs only 7 percent of classification accuracy, while image-independent increments predict the next query with R^2 = 0.98 (held out). Our results suggest that the CTM has found a single strategy to process all ImageNet images.

♻ ☆ Progressive Lower Bound Evaluation for Urban Road Renovation Scheduling
Robbert Bosch, Patricia Rogetzer, Wouter van Heeswijk, Martijn Mes
Urban infrastructure degrades over time, necessitating periodic renovation to maintain functionality and safety. When renovation is delayed beyond the infrastructure's remaining lifespan, costly emergency interventions become necessary to prevent failure. Decision makers must therefore balance expected emergency intervention costs against traffic congestion impacts. We formalize this trade-off as a road network maintenance scheduling problem with uncertain deadlines, which presents optimization challenges including computationally expensive evaluation and an exponentially growing solution space. We formulate the problem as a bi-level multi-objective optimization problem that explicitly accounts for uncertain infrastructure lifespans through probabilistic failure models. We develop a progressive lower bound evaluation method: candidate schedules receive quick, optimistic estimates of their traffic impact from machine learning based surrogate models, and these estimates are refined by exact traffic simulation only for promising candidates, so that full evaluation is reserved almost exclusively for schedules that can advance the Pareto front. Embedded in a multi-objective genetic algorithm, this evaluation strategy improves solution quality by enabling many more iterations within a fixed computational budget. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness and scalability on substantially larger problem instances than previously addressed in the literature: 76 and 80 projects on the Sioux Falls and Anaheim networks, respectively. Under an identical 24-hour computational budget across 30 random seeds, the method completes up to 87 times as many optimization iterations as standard NSGA-II and achieves statistically significant improvements across multiple performance metrics over both standard NSGA-II and a surrogate-assisted baseline.

Our worked linear-Gaussian update connects posterior computation to error and a distribution-shift decision. Recent results from Urschel bound elimination growth probabilistically under distinct Gaussian-input and random-preconditioning hypotheses. Our unique approach to warm rotation binds candidate parameters to their numerical evidence and destination while each request observes a coherent model and state. We propose Bayesian distillation as a source of prior information. Our architecture offers a route to domain computations with explicit guarantees that can guide automated decisions and model responses. We specify experiments to evaluate prediction quality, domain errors across conversational turns, and total resource cost.

☆ Duration-Aware World Models for Sleep Staging with Dwell-Time Constraints
Junhui Gao
Closed-loop neuromodulation requires sleep staging that respects stage-specific minimum dwells: stimulation policies switch by sleep stage, and a policy change is permitted only after the current stage has persisted for its minimum duration. Discriminative classifiers fragment stage trajectories---for example, a 30 s Wake segment inside a 10 min N2 run---and even hidden semi-Markov smoothing leaves 11.3% of segments below the minimum dwell threshold. This paper presents a world model in which a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) learns dwell structure endogenously from EEG, via duration-aware latent sampling, a survival-curve dwell prior, and transition-matrix calibration, and a trajectory-level hard-constraint layer guarantees the minimum dwell at decoding. On SHHS-1 (200 subjects, 160/20/20, three repeated splits), the model reaches a test accuracy of 0.690 +/- 0.053 (95% CI over 3 folds) versus 0.641 +/- 0.042 for an identically split discriminative baseline, with macro-F1 +17.5 pp and better accuracy on all three folds. On Sleep-EDF the constraint layer cuts below-threshold segments from 71.8% to 0.1% with no accuracy loss (0.734 to 0.737), and an online locked scheduler reduces RL policy switches by 87% per night while keeping every policy run at least 90 s. To the best of the author's knowledge, this is the first system to couple learned dwell statistics with a decoding-time hard guarantee. Code and pretrained weights will be released.

☆ Controlling the latency in temporal coded spiking models for neuromorphic datasets
Alban Gattepaille, Alexandre Muzy
Exploiting temporal information in datasets with high temporal dependencies (such as spoken keyword recognition) by spiking models is still an open problem. Promising frameworks include Time-To-First coding (TTFS) and the inclusion of synaptic delays into learning. In TTFS, neurons are forced to spike at most once, forcing the network to found its learning on the spiking times of neurons rather than their spiking rate. Some models use the TTFS framework to directly compute the spiking time of Integrate-and-Fire (IF) or Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons. However, most models built in the TTFS framework have not been tested against datasets containing temporal information. Little is known about the latency of these models on temporal datasets, where the latency is the time taken by the network to correctly classify a sample. In this work, we study the behaviour of Delay Neural Networks (DeNN) models, i.e. models that directly compute the spiking time of neurons by bypassing the membrane potential and thresholding mechanisms of spiking neurons. We show how to analytically control their latency, and empirically study the latency-accuracy tradeoff in a dynamic temporal dataset.

This study tests whether the name predicts the result. On ZDT test functions the same NSGA-II implementations differed up to 470-fold in IGD. An ablation in one open-source NSGA-II reproduced the behaviour of one tool from its documented settings but not the gaps of the other two, so documented parameters do not identify an implementation. Counting the budget in wall-clock time reversed the ranking of the model-based optimizer, and reporting the final population instead of the archive understated some configurations by up to a third; most differences fell below the surrogate's error. For optimizers embedded in design-support systems, the implementation is part of the method; a reporting checklist is derived: implementation and version, effective settings, budget in time and evaluations, and archive-based indicators.
