☆ Design and Analysis of Temporal Representations in Neural Networks
Alban Colas-Gattepaille, Alexandre Muzy
The ability to represent temporal information is often hypothesized to underlie the efficiency and learning capabilities of biological neural networks. This motivates the development of spiking neural networks. However, it remains unclear how temporal information is actually represented in neural networks and how different forms of temporal representation affect performance and computational efficiency. We introduce the notion of the degree of temporal representation of a neural network, defined by whether its constituent functions (activation, learning, encoding, and decoding) explicitly manipulate time as a computational variable. This perspective yields a continuum ranging from non-temporal representations, where time does not explicitly appear as a computational variable in the network functions, to fully temporal representations, where computations explicitly operate on temporal variables. Using a fixed deep architecture, we compare different encoding, activation mechanisms and decoding with increasing temporal expressiveness: non-temporal weighted-sum activations used in usual artificial neural networks, non-temporal binary spiking activations used in spiking neural networks, and spike-time-based activations used in delay neural networks. Experiments on event-based datasets show that increasing the degree of temporal representation improves both performance and computational efficiency, allowing state-of-the-art performances on the Google Speech Commands dataset. We further analyze how temporal representations induce distinct forward and backward computational trajectories, leading to gradients that depend explicitly on the history of event times.
☆ A Time-Variant Spiking Neuron from a Unified State-Dynamics Perspective
Jing Yang, Qianhui Liu, Gang Pan, Zhanglu Yan
Spiking neural networks (SNNs) have increasingly incorporated rich neuronal dynamics to enhance temporal processing. However, richer dynamics do not necessarily enable neurons to adapt how information is processed over time. To examine this issue systematically, we introduce a unified state-dynamics framework that characterizes diverse spiking neurons through a common formulation and enables direct comparison of their dynamical designs. The framework reveals a common limitation of existing neurons: although they enhance temporal processing through richer internal states and state evolution, the dynamical rules determining how inputs are integrated, how states evolve, and how they are read out generally remain unchanged throughout temporal processing. Such time-invariant rules limit the ability of neurons to adjust information processing as information relevance changes over time. Inspired by time-varying regulation in biological neurons, we propose the Time-Variant Multi-Compartment Neuron (TV-MCN). TV-MCN builds on multiscale compartment dynamics and makes the rules for input integration, state evolution, and state readout time-varying according to the current input. Specifically, an input-dependent internal time regulates the rate of state evolution, while the current input dynamically modulates input integration and state readout. Extensive experiments show that TV-MCN achieves strong overall performance, with particularly large gains on tasks requiring selective retention and retrieval of information, while ablation studies further support the effectiveness of its time-varying mechanisms.
☆ How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron? Resolution-Dependent Interaction Order and Computational Capacity
Nima Dehghani
Mandlebrot's coastline paradox reframes measurement as a joint property of an object and its ruler. Here we ask how observational resolution shapes the apparent structure of neural computation. We introduce a scale-indexed decomposition that separates the predictive information captured by direct dependencies from the residual outside that model family. Exact constructions show that projection can convert higher-order dependence into pairwise structure. Projection can increase the direct fraction of surviving information even as total predictive information decreases. A schematic branch-to-soma cascade grounds these effects in local coincidence detection, saturating integration and somatic mixing. Resolving organized nonlinear subunits improves approximation and raises effective representational rank. In a nested hierarchy, these gains occur without increasing information about the target. This distinction separates information availability from access by a restricted readout. A point-neuron or direct population model therefore establishes an effective description at a specified scale. It does not uniquely identify the finer computation that generated the observed relation. Which resolution is adequate depends on the observable and perturbation of interest.
♻ ☆ T-GADE: Thermodynamical Generative-AI-Driven Evolution of LLM Artifacts

We tested an implementation example aligned with Evolution of Heuristics (EoH) on the online bin-packing task, where the excess is the bin count in excess of the volume lower bound, relative to that bound. The HoxLM-equipped configuration reached lower excess with fewer total LLM calls than EoH. In the preregistered comparison at 400 total calls it won 9 of 10 seed-paired runs, with a median sealed excess of 0.836% against 3.912%, and it was also better in the mean and in the worst case. Temperature controls the spread of the retained population under both update schemes, and a small positive temperature improves training quality over the collapsed $T=0$ point in the generational Bose-type scheme. ♻ ☆ PotentialEP: Backprop-Free Training of CIFAR-Scale Generative Models via Equilibrium Propagation
Alex Gower
Generating an image with a diffusion or flow-matching model typically involves integrating a velocity field for hundreds of sequential steps. That computation suits a GPU poorly and an analog neuromorphic substrate well, where one fast, low-power physical relaxation could replace the whole sequence. Two things are needed: a generative algorithm whose computation is a relaxation, and a way to train it without backpropagation, whose global gradient transport is hard to realise in analog. Energy Matching supplies the first, sampling by gradient-descent relaxation on a time-independent potential - but obtaining the gradient that descent follows is itself a backward pass, once per integration step. We prove that a predictive coding network with a single linear injection term added to its energy relaxes to a state whose visible layer carries that gradient inherently, with an error that vanishes for small injection strengths. An Energy Matching model trained by backpropagation can therefore be loaded into this network unchanged and sampled by relaxation alone, matching the original model's FID to within 0.04 at CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 scale. The network can also be trained without backpropagation: Equilibrium Propagation reproduces backpropagation's parameter updates to a cosine similarity of 0.9998, and training end to end with those updates reaches an FID of 3.64 on unconditional CIFAR-10 against 3.54 for backpropagation. To our knowledge this is the first CIFAR-10 generative model trained with Equilibrium Propagation, and the first at competitive quality by any backpropagation-free rule. This quality does not require group normalisation or attention: an architecture of only convolutions and pointwise nonlinearities, both native to an analog crossbar, reaches an FID of 3.51 when trained by backpropagation.

♻ ☆ Position: Hippocampal Explicit Memory Is the Cornerstone for AGI ICML 2026
Sangjun Park
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various tasks, raising expectations for Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). This position paper argues that integrating explicit memory is the cornerstone for advancing LLMs toward AGI. The key reason is that the underlying learning mechanism of LLMs is highly analogous to human implicit memory. However, higher-order cognitive functions necessary for AGI, such as long-term strategic planning, metacognition, and symbolic reasoning, heavily rely on hippocampal explicit memory and cannot arise solely from implicit statistical learning. Drawing on findings from neuroscience, I advance this perspective and complement it with computational requirements for artificial explicit memory systems, hoping to foster further research and lay the groundwork for explicit memory integration.

☆ LLM Evolutionary Search Strategies Should be Compared by Tokens
Tal Oved, Roi Pony, Oshri Naparstek, Udi Barzelay
LLM evolutionary search is currently evaluated by counting proposals (candidate programs). We demonstrate this metric hides the true cost of search, and redo the comparison using tokens. By replaying 600 logged runs across 5 tasks and 3 methods, we show that proposal costs vary wildly from 16k to 39k tokens. In equal-proposal comparisons, this silently grants some methods up to 1.9x the compute of others, and gives evolution roughly 6x the budget of independent sampling. When we match token budgets, giving sampling six times more attempts, and remove scorer exploits, the evolutionary advantage largely vanishes. Evolution beats independent sampling by 5% or less on 12 of 15 task-method pairs, retaining a 23 to 28% margin on only 3, all on one task. A replication with Claude Haiku 4.5 reproduces this split, though a third backbone shows its size depends on the model too. The performance margin justifying these systems is often an accounting artifact. Reporting tokens, not proposals and not model calls, fixes this and costs nothing, as the logs already hold them.
☆ Same Function, Different Trajectory: No Standard Optimizer Is Equivariant to Transformer Reparameterization

We show that two Transformers representing the same function can follow different training trajectories. For example, doubling a query matrix and halving its key matrix preserves the model's function but changes the gradient scales seen by the optimizer. Our theoretical analysis establishes that standard block-local first-order optimizers fail to scale updates with parameters under a shared learning rate. For AdamW, transforming the first- and second-moment estimates alone does not correct the mismatch between parameter and update scales. To make runs restarted from equivalent checkpoints follow the same trajectory, we balance matrix pairs and transform their moment estimates together, bringing distinct but equivalent training states to the same starting point. To correct scale imbalance between paired Transformer matrices without changing predictions, we propose Symmetry-Aware Gradient Geometry Stabilization (SAGGS), which periodically equalizes the Frobenius norms of exact symmetry pairs, and its damped variant, Soft SAGGS. SAGGS reduces perplexity (PPL) by $0.374\pm0.026$ at 101M parameters on WikiText-103, and Soft SAGGS reduces PPL by $0.780\pm0.040$ in a 31M modern-architecture replication, both under scale imbalance. In a 123.8M checkpoint-resume experiment, reciprocally rescaling matrix pairs barely changes validation loss at restart but increases final PPL by $3.78\pm0.42$; hard and soft rebalancing recover to within $0.02$ PPL of the control.

To explain how these mechanisms maintain scale consistency, we introduce Neural Dimensional Analysis (NDA), a unified framework based on dimensional consistency. We define neural units that specify how tensors rescale and which quantities can be added, just as physical units do in physics. Our rules match residual units, nondimensionalize attention and gate inputs, combine losses across units, and convert gradient units into parameter units. GCT's normalized residual stream also shows improved robustness to quantization. At 1B parameters, calibrated per-tensor int8 quantization increases GCT's validation loss by only 0.009 nats, compared with up to 5.51 nats for the baselines. Vision and physics-informed neural network experiments further confirm NDA's benefits beyond language modeling. These results establish dimensional consistency as a neural network design principle.

Simple aggregation of independent responses ("wisdom of crowds") generally improves collective performance through statistical facilitation, but interaction among members can sometimes hinder group outcomes. However, under certain circumstances, coordination studies show that interacting groups can outperform their individual members and nominal groups, and interaction can also be more efficient than independence. We present a reservoir computing model to investigate how interaction can enhance joint performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Echo state networks were trained independently to identify Japanese speakers from vowel recordings and tested jointly with and without coupled feedback. Model pairs reproduced the dyadic advantage reported by Bahrami et al. (2010) with interaction via pooled-feedback, but not when independent responses were aggregated together. Model dynamics revealed that interaction was beneficial whereas aggregated outputs were prone to diverging from runaway feedback over time. In terms of efficiency, larger groups of smaller interacting models outperformed smaller groups of larger models while equating for total amount of group computation. Our results offer a formal framework for explaining when and why interaction enhances collective intelligence.

Even when a previously successful policy is retained, it may no longer provide a reliable starting point for rapid adaptation after interference, reflecting a form of \emph{loss of plasticity} that single-policy preservation cannot address. Inspired by quality-diversity methods, we introduce \textsc{TeLAPA} (Transfer-Enabled Latent-Aligned Policy Archives), a continual RL framework that organizes behaviorally diverse policy neighborhoods into per-task archives and maintains a shared latent space so that archived policies remain comparable and reusable under non-stationary drift. This perspective shifts continual RL from retaining isolated solutions to maintaining \emph{skill-aligned neighborhoods} with competent and behaviorally related policies that support future relearning. In our MiniGrid CL setting, \textsc{TeLAPA} learns more tasks successfully, recovers competence faster on revisited tasks after interference, and retains higher performance across a sequence of tasks. Our analyses show that source-optimal policies are often not transfer-optimal, even within a local competent neighborhood, and that effective reuse depends on retaining and selecting among multiple nearby alternatives rather than collapsing them to one representative. Together, these results reframe continual RL around reusable and competent policy neighborhoods, providing a route beyond single-model preservation toward more plastic lifelong agents.
♻ ☆ Distribution Matching Evolutionary Algorithms for Rare Event Sampling
Yonatan Gideoni, Yarin Gal
A novel discovery is one which is both useful and surprising: a generative model's output is a useful discovery if it has a low probability of being generated (it's surprising) and a high reward (it's useful). Global optimization can directly increase the probability of sampling high rewards but typically requires updating model weights. Such gradient based optimization is expensive and bars using capable closed-source models. Instead, modern search methods for discovery sacrifice the global target, and use evolutionary algorithms with local reward maximizing objectives, permitting the search to focus only on high probability samples. In this paper, we interpret various evolutionary algorithms as approximate Markov Chain Monte Carlo, an optimization-free method to sample from complex distributions. This interpretation allows developing Distribution Matching Evolutionary Algorithms (DME), a class of search methods which sample from a global target distribution without updating weights. Empirically, DME has a higher sample efficiency than existing methods on problems requiring many samples to find a solution.

☆ FidLIF: Parallel Training of High-Fidelity Spiking Neurons with Exact BPTT
Kaixiang He, Yujie Wu
Although spiking neural networks (SNNs) show promise in energy-efficient computing through event-driven computation and stateful temporal processing, their recurrent membrane dynamics render their training inherently sequential and inefficient for long sequences. Existing methods achieve full-sequence parallelism in SNNs through two main strategies: redesigning or approximating spiking dynamics to avoid reset-coupled temporal dependencies, or relying on iterative relaxed fixed-point solvers that suffer from excessive memory costs and iteration-dependent backward overhead. To address these limitations, we present FidLIF, a novel framework that reconciles the incremental update and hard-reset behavior of standard spiking LIF neurons with parallel forward propagation and BPTT-equivalent backward propagation. FidLIF iteratively recovers the full-sequence membrane-potential trajectory in parallel. By exploiting the lower bidiagonal structure induced by the local recurrence of LIF neurons, FidLIF formulates each forward trajectory correction and backward adjoint propagation as associative scans with an $O(\log T)$ temporal depth. This formulation also supports input-dependent neuronal parameters and allows the same neuron to perform full-sequence parallel training and incremental step-by-step inference at deployment. In our numerical convergence evaluation, FidLIF achieves a mean absolute error below $10^{-7}$ relative to the matched serial relaxed LIF dynamics, while yielding gradients numerically equivalent to exact BPTT. Our Triton implementation delivers favorable long-sequence latency and memory scaling, while achieving competitive performance on four sequential classification benchmarks. By reconciling parallel training with step-by-step execution, FidLIF enables high-fidelity spiking dynamics to benefit from parallel hardware without compromising incremental inference at deployment.

Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in decoding performance in both cross-session and cross-subject settings. Existing models of learning in the brain explain how given circuits learn, but not how biology could assemble those circuits in the first place. To address this gap, we formulate Self-Assembling Learning (SAL)---the study of how learning systems can emerge from lower-level interactions---and introduce one example mechanism, the Self-Assembling Motif (SAM). SAM is self-assembling at two scales: the motif emerges from initially random connectivity under heterosynaptic plasticity rules, and networks of SAMs, composed hierarchically, self-organize into dynamics that provably approximate a generalized form of stochastic gradient descent---matching backpropagation-level performance. This suggests that biological learning need not be prescribed but can emerge from local rules---and to a far greater extent than previously thought.

♻ ☆ AutoPSO: A Meta-framework for Automated Particle Swarm Optimization

Particle swarm optimization (PSO) is a widely used metaheuristic, prized for its simplicity and small parameter set. Although decades of research have produced numerous PSO variants that improve performance by modifying key components (e.g., parameter schedules, swarm topologies, or updating rules), two fundamental challenges persist. First, most existing approaches are problem-specific and hand-crafted, leading to poor cross-task generalization and forcing practitioners to navigate an impractically large design space, which also hinders systematic reuse of prior effective mechanisms. Second, mainstream implementations remain CPU-bound, constraining scalability and substantially increasing computational cost in real-world applications. To address these challenges, we propose AutoPSO, a highly automated meta-framework for constructing customized PSO algorithms. AutoPSO formulates PSO-based optimization as a bi-level process: an outer search explores the joint space of effective PSO components, while an inner loop instantiates candidate variants to solve the target task and provide feedback. The outer search operates over a curated, open-design component pool, supporting flexible replacement of the component set and the outer optimizer. Crucially, by leveraging EvoX for population tensorization and batched evaluations, AutoPSO can efficiently assess thousands of particles within practical time budgets. Comprehensive experiments on numerical benchmarks and neuroevolution robotic control tasks demonstrate that AutoPSO consistently discovers novel PSO variants that significantly outperform strong baselines. Ablation and scalability studies further highlight the contribution of individual algorithmic components and confirm that AutoPSO achieves increasing performance gains with larger swarm sizes. Code is available at {https://github.com/EMI-Group/autopso}.

This paper proposes a solution to address this gap: the NeuroRule knowledge distillation framework that results in explainable rule-sets from neural network models. NeuroRule adapts the EVOTER rule-set evolution infrastructure to treat neural networks as targets for the evolution process, distilling their performance into concise sets of propositional logic expressions. There are three primary contributions: (1) an evolutionary method for distilling black-box neural network models into explicit rule-set models; (2) a method for making rule sets more explainable by including a conciseness objective to evolution; and (3) a demonstration that the distillation is viable even without access to the original neural network training data. The paper thus establishes that black-box neural network models can be made explainable and therefore useful in real-world applications where trustworthiness is paramount.

Abrar Alotaibi, Moataz Ahmed
Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to adversarial prompts that bypass their safety training. Existing automated red-teaming methods either require privileged access unavailable in production, rely on manually engineered per-model templates, or optimize a single objective without population-level diversity. We catalog REPRO's behavior on AdvBench, JailbreakBench, and HarmBench across 36 target models from 11 families, including GPT-5-nano, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and Grok-4.1. Under our protocol REPRO reaches 100\% attack success rate (ASR) on every evaluated target in a single turn, at a median of 24 target queries per behavior. Two properties of the protocol qualify that figure. The judge scoring candidates during optimization also produces the reported ASR, and search halts when it accepts, so ASR reports whether search succeeded within the iteration budget rather than success at a fixed budget. All baseline figures are transcribed from their original papers, which use different judges, budgets, and model versions. We therefore present this as a catalog of model coverage under one protocol rather than a head-to-head ranking, and develop both qualifications in the paper.

Ziteng Sui, Junfeng Xia, Wenhao Ye, Mo Wang, Quanying Liu
Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) commonly characterizes large-scale brain organization through functional connectivity (FC). However, an observed FC matrix is not a fixed brain graph but a statistical estimate determined by the finite BOLD frames used to compute it. Conventional FC-based approaches typically represent each scan with a single Pearson-correlation matrix, leaving frame-resolved variations in regional interactions unexploited. To address this limitation, we introduce CoFlu-Brain, which organizes framewise cofluctuation observations into multiple retained and dropped views, each summarized as an FC matrix. The model learns connectivity structure reproducible across retained views and predicts the representations of the corresponding dropped views, while adopting SIGReg from LeJEPA to prevent representation collapse. We pretrained CoFlu-Brain on 13,444 subjects from eight dataset groups and evaluated its representations via frozen-encoder linear probing on seven classification and two age-prediction tasks across seven datasets. CoFlu-Brain showed strong transfer across demographic, developmental, and clinical prediction tasks, outperforming the evaluated released models on most tasks. Random frame partitioning improved aggregate transfer, while the complete objective achieved the strongest overall performance. Code is available.

Efficient neural architecture search (NAS) requires accurate performance estimation under limited evaluation budgets. By providing a fast, reliable, and structurally simple evaluation mechanism, FENAS supports the design of automated neural architectures under limited evaluation budgets.

Results demonstrate Spiketrum's superiority in most benchmarking criteria, making it a promising choice for various applications. Analyses of grokking usually read hidden activations in one basis, most often the Fourier basis modulo $p$. We ask how much the answer to "has the network organised yet?" depends on that choice. The measure FSD$_{\rm gen}$ averages each unit's activation over inputs with the same answer and counts how many units share the same strongest irreducible representation. For modular multiplication we read one answer-averaged profile in three orders: discrete-logarithm order, in which the characters of the multiplicative group become Fourier modes; natural order; and random orders. Across 60 networks at $p\in\{59,97,113\}$, the discrete-log reading reached a fixed threshold before both other readings in 60 of 60 networks (59 of 60 when it had to hold 500 steps). Because untrained networks already score higher in discrete-log order, we also required an equal rise above each reading's untrained level; the discrete-log reading was still first in at least 16 of 20 networks at every prime. At $p=59$ and $p=97$ this happened during the memorisation plateau in 35 of 39 networks; at $p=113$ in 12 of 20. Memorisation preceded grokking in all 179 runs that grokked, by more than any synchronisation signal on average, so a lead over grokking is not by itself evidence of a detected circuit. Synchronisation time is only weakly related to grokking time (pooled $ρ=0.18$). On six finite groups, read with the same measure in every basis, the irreducible-representation reading came before random element orders on all six; with equal-rise thresholds this held in every case on four groups, in 7 of 10 on $\mathbb{Z}_5\times\mathbb{Z}_5$ and in none on $D_{16}$, where about half the profile power lies in one-dimensional representations the measure leaves out. ♻ ☆ Neuromorphic Computing Based on Parametrically-Driven Oscillators and Frequency Combs
Mahadev Sunil Kumar, Adarsh Ganesan
Parametrically driven oscillators exhibit distinct dynamical regimes that strongly influence their computational capability as physical reservoirs. Here, we demonstrate reservoir computing in a two-mode system exhibiting 2:1 parametric resonance using Mackey--Glass, Rössler, and Lorenz chaotic time-series prediction tasks. Mapping the normalized mean squared error over parameter space reveals that the lowest prediction errors consistently occur within the parametric resonance regime, where nonlinear interactions are activated while temporal coherence is preserved. In contrast, although frequency-comb states increase spectral dimensionality, prediction performance degrades in the chaotic comb regime due to loss of phase coherence. We further show that the modulation depth $Δ\text{F}$, detuning $κ$, damping ratio $γ_{21}$, and input data rate systematically reshape the accessible dynamical regimes and thereby control the reservoir performance. These results identify parametric resonance as a robust operating regime for oscillator-based neuromorphic computing and establish dynamical regime engineering as a route toward physical reservoir optimization.

♻ ☆ Employing Discrete Fourier Transform in Representation Learning
Raoof HojatJalali, Edmondo Trentin
Image representation learning via input reconstruction is a common technique in machine learning for generating representations that can be effectively utilized by arbitrary downstream tasks. A well-established approach uses autoencoders to extract latent representations at the network's compression point. These representations are valuable because they retain essential information necessary for reconstructing the original input from the compressed latent space. In this paper, we propose an alternative learning objective. Instead of using the raw input as the reconstruction target, we employ the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) of the input. The DFT provides meaningful global information at each frequency level, making individual frequency components useful as separate learning targets. When dealing with multidimensional input data, the DFT offers remarkable flexibility by enabling selective transformation across specific dimensions while preserving others in the computation. Moreover, certain types of input exhibit distinct patterns in their frequency distributions, where specific frequency components consistently contain most of the magnitude, allowing us to focus on a subset of frequencies rather than the entire spectrum. These characteristics position the DFT as a viable learning objective for representation learning. We validate our approach on the CIFAR-10 and STL-10 datasets under constrained training regimes. We discovered that integrating data augmentation during pretraining enhances the learned representations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that training exclusively on the lower-frequency components, those containing the highest magnitudes, produces results comparable to using the full frequency spectrum with only minimal reductions in accuracy.

☆ RELAGRAM: Recursive Latent Graph Model for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem NeurIPS 2026
Vladimir Kirill Bickov, Neil Yorke-Smith
Latent recursion repeatedly processes internal representations through the same neural network. Recent work has shown this approach to be effective on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and maze solving. However, whether latent recursion can support neural routing remains unclear. We introduce RELAGRAM (Recursive Latent Graph Model), a novel approach that brings latent recursion to graph combinatorial optimization. RELAGRAM encodes a capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) instance as edge tokens; a compact transformer recurrently updates the latent representations of these tokens. An output head maps the answer state to an edge heatmap, from which an autoregressive decoder constructs a feasible solution. On CVRP-100 instances, the 0.53M-parameter RELAGRAM achieves gaps to a PyVRP reference of 13.4%, 9.8%, and 8.3% under greedy decoding, eightfold symmetry augmentation, and 256-candidate search, respectively. Trained only on CVRP-100, RELAGRAM generalizes zero-shot to CVRP-500 and CVRP-1000, achieving gaps of 15.6% and 21.7% under 256-candidate search. Together, these results demonstrate that latent recursion is a promising approach to neural routing.

♻ ☆ When LLMs Develop Languages: Symbolic Communication for Efficient Multi-Agent Reasoning ICML2026
Zhengqi Pei, Qingming Huang, Shuhui Wang
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) improves large language models (LLMs) on difficult reasoning tasks, but it often incurs long natural-language rationales that are poorly aligned with efficient machine reasoning. We propose Communicative Language Symbolism Routing (CLSR), a test-time framework in which multiple LLM agents autonomously invent, evolve, and share compact Language Symbolism Frameworks (LSFs), while a latent-free router adaptively selects and composes these languages per query to optimize the accuracy-token trade-off. Unlike prompt optimization that refines surface instructions, CLSR treats each LSF as a reusable symbolic protocol with compact symbols, usage rules, and a message-passing contract, and improves it through an evolutionary loop driven by correctness and token cost. At inference time, the router may invoke a single low-cost LSF call, ensemble multiple LSFs, or execute a multi-round LSF composition protocol on harder queries. Across challenging benchmarks, CLSR reduces latency-oriented generated token completion by $3\sim 6\times$ compared to standard CoT while maintaining accuracy. We further derive an information-theoretic lower bound on token cost under arbitrary symbolism and show that, under an interpreter-realizability premise, multi-round LSF protocols conditionally subsume program-execution pipelines. Code is publicly available (https://github.com/pzqpzq/LSF_MDia).

With an estimated candidate-training cost of 132 V100 GPU-days, the search uncovers multiple native SNN architectures, exemplified by three designs featuring mechanisms such as spike-activity-dependent control of state updates and residual pathways. The discovered NeuroGate surpasses the ANN DeltaNet on WikiText-103, and the discovered architectures reduce estimated architecture-level arithmetic energy by up to 50.6x (LoopMem) relative to a common dense Transformer (ANN) baseline. ☆ Do Artificial Neural Networks Need Dendritic Nanotubes? Two Reasons for Shrinking Importance Estimates in Continual Learning
Saurav K. Aryal
Regularization-based continual learning protects each parameter in proportion to an estimate of its importance, yet these estimates come from finite samples and heuristics and are used as if they were exact. We report four studies that start from a biologically inspired mechanism and end with a statistical explanation of it. Motivated by dendritic nanotubes, we let transient lateral links diffuse importance tags between hidden units. Links between co-active units gave no significant gain, but random links with lifetimes of 25 or 200 steps raised final accuracy on 20-task Permuted MNIST by 1.5 to 2.6 points. We show that random diffusion implements linear shrinkage of importance toward the layer mean in expectation. A simulation of the link process alone predicts shrinkage weights of 0.23 and 0.52 for these lifetimes, and graph-free shrinkage at 0.25 and 0.5 reproduces both the accuracy and the dispersion of the consolidated importance, while every activity-dependent rule did worse than random links. A five-seed screen across EWC, SI, and MAS found nominal gains for SI and MAS on Permuted MNIST and losses on task-incremental Split CIFAR-100, where forgetting was small and shrinkage cost plasticity. Varying the number of importance samples then separates two mechanisms on Permuted MNIST. For EWC, the gain fell by about ten points per tenfold increase in samples, from 19.6 points with 10 samples to -0.4 with 1000, a variance effect. For MAS, a gain of about one point persisted at 1000 samples, consistent with a bias in the importance measure rather than noise. Shrinkage had no detectable effect for MAS on a domain-incremental CIFAR-100 benchmark. Finally, we show that a standard heteroscedastic empirical Bayes rule shrinks the largest Fisher-type estimates most, which may explain its poor results, and point to a log-scale alternative.

♻ ☆ The Value of Spike Timing: A Leakage-Resistant Benchmark of SNN Design Choices for Network Intrusion Detection
Raj Patel, Shaswata Mitra, David Amebley, Taye Akinrele, Sayanton Dibbo, Sudip Mittal, Shahram Rahimi
Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are increasingly studied for network intrusion detection, but comparative evidence on how neuron models and spike encodings affect performance remains limited. Evaluation choices can further influence the observed results when preprocessing, capture structure, or scenario information crosses the train-test boundary. We evaluate nine snnTorch neuron families with three spike encodings, yielding 27 SNN configurations across four intrusion-detection benchmarks. We first screen the complete design space and then repeat the evaluation using train-only transforms, seed-independent partitions, and capture- or scenario-aware separation. At the shared operating point, LeakyParallel/latency achieved the lowest mean rank in both sweeps but was not statistically separated from Leaky/latency; their screening order reversed when CTU-13 was excluded. Overall, screening and confirmation retained substantial rank agreement despite changes in measured performance. We then examine what latency coding contributes by holding the active spike set fixed and changing only its temporal organization. At the main T=25 operating point, mapping feature magnitude to spike time improved macro-F1 on all five confirmation protocols, while spreading the same spikes through time without that mapping could either improve or reduce performance. Latency coding thus combines informative spike timing with temporal network dynamics. Sparse input encoding does not directly imply sparse internal activity, although latency coding requires fewer fanout-weighted operations than rate coding in the evaluated models. These findings motivate separate assessment of SNN design, evaluation protocol, spike timing, and computational activity for static network-flow data.
